summary.text: For $p\equiv3\pmod4$, rows and suitably signed columns are reindexed by the nonzero quadratic residues, turning the matrix into a mixture of commuting skew-symmetric and symmetric Paley matrices; a parity count gives an odd skew-symmetric principal block, so its determinant vanishes. For $p\equiv1\pmod4$, Euler’s criterion reduces the determinant modulo $p$ to $\det((i^2-m!j)^m)$, whose binomial/Vandermonde factorization is nonsingular; Wilson’s theorem, via $(m!)^2=-1$, rules out the remaining scalar obstruction.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
p=p_n,\qquad m=\frac{p-1}{2},\qquad C=m!,
\]
and let \(\chi=\left(\frac{\cdot}{p}\right)\) be the quadratic character of \(\mathbf F_p\), extended by \(\chi(0)=0\). Thus the integer matrix whose determinant is \(a(n)\) is
\[
L=(L_{ij})_{1\leq i,j\leq m},\qquad
L_{ij}=\chi(i^2-Cj).
\]
We prove that, for every odd prime \(p\),
\[
\det L=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p\equiv3\pmod4. \tag{1}
\]
The asserted statement for the sequence follows because, when \(n\geq2\), the \(n\)-th prime is odd. (The convention in the statement writes it as the zero-indexed prime \(\operatorname{nthPrime}(n-1)\).)

We first establish two pieces of linear algebra that will be used in the two congruence classes.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1. A mixed-column skew-symmetry lemma

Let \(K\) be a field of characteristic zero, let \(I\) be a finite index set, and suppose that \(A,B\in M_I(K)\) satisfy
\[
A^T=-A,\qquad B^T=B,\qquad AB=BA. \tag{2}
\]
If \(S\subseteq I\) has odd cardinality, form a matrix \(D\) by taking column \(j\) from \(A\) when \(j\in S\), and from \(B\) when \(j\notin S\). Then
\[
\det D=0. \tag{3}
\]

First suppose that \(B\) is invertible and put \(T=B^{-1}A\). The commutation in (2) implies that \(A\) also commutes with \(B^{-1}\). Consequently
\[
T^T=A^T(B^{-1})^T=(-A)B^{-1}=-B^{-1}A=-T.
\]
Multiplying \(D\) on the left by \(B^{-1}\), its columns outside \(S\) become the corresponding columns of the identity matrix, while its columns in \(S\) become those of \(T\). If rows and columns are simultaneously ordered with the elements of \(S\) first, this matrix has block form
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
T_{S,S}&0\\
T_{I\setminus S,S}&I
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Its determinant is therefore \(\det T_{S,S}\). The principal submatrix \(T_{S,S}\) is skew-symmetric and has odd size. Hence
\[
\det T_{S,S}=\det T_{S,S}^T=\det(-T_{S,S})=(-1)^{|S|}\det T_{S,S}=-\det T_{S,S},
\]
so it is zero in characteristic zero. Since multiplication by \(B^{-1}\) changes the determinant by a nonzero factor, \(\det D=0\).

For a possibly singular \(B\), introduce an indeterminate \(X\) and replace \(B\) by
\[
B_X=B+XI.
\]
Over the rational function field \(K(X)\), this matrix is invertible: \(\det(B+XI)\) is a monic polynomial in \(X\) of degree \(|I|\), hence is not the zero polynomial. It remains symmetric and commutes with \(A\). The preceding argument says that the mixed-column determinant formed from \(A\) and \(B_X\) is zero in \(K(X)\), and therefore is the zero polynomial in \(K[X]\). Evaluating at \(X=0\) proves (3).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2. Paley matrices on the nonzero quadratic residues

We need the preceding lemma for a particular pair of matrices. Let \(F\) be a finite field of odd characteristic and suppose
\[
\chi(-1)=-1,
\]
where \(\chi\) is its quadratic character. Let
\[
Q=\{r\in F:\chi(r)=1\}
\]
be the set of nonzero squares. Define rational matrices indexed by \(Q\) by
\[
A_{rs}=\chi(r-s),\qquad B_{rs}=\chi(r+s). \tag{4}
\]
Here the character values \(0,\pm1\) are regarded as rational numbers. We claim
\[
A^T=-A,\qquad B^T=B,
\qquad AB=BA. \tag{5}
\]
The first two identities are immediate: since \(s-r=-(r-s)\), multiplicativity and \(\chi(-1)=-1\) give \(\chi(s-r)=-\chi(r-s)\), including the diagonal where both sides are zero; and addition is symmetric.

We give the character-sum argument for commutativity. We use the standard quadratic-character correlation
\[
\sum_{x\in F}\chi(x-a)\chi(x-b)=
\begin{cases}
|F|-1,&a=b,\\
-1,&a\ne b.
\end{cases} \tag{6}
\]
For completeness, when \(a=b\), every nonzero summand is \(1\), and the single zero summand is \(0\). When \(a\ne b\), substitute \(x=a+(b-a)y\). The factors \(\chi(b-a)^2=1\) cancel, reducing the sum to \(\sum_y\chi(y)\chi(y-1)=-1\). The latter is the elementary quadratic Jacobi sum; it also follows by counting solutions to a quadratic equation (equivalently, the Jacobi sum of the nontrivial quadratic character with its inverse equals \(-\chi(-1)\), followed by replacing \(1-y\) with \(-(y-1)\)).

Fix \(r,t\in Q\) and set
\[
f(x)=\chi(r-x)\chi(x+t).
\]
Because \(r\ne-t\)—otherwise the square \(r\) would be the negative of the square \(t\), contrary to \(\chi(-1)=-1\)—formula (6) gives
\[
\sum_{x\in F}f(x)=1. \tag{7}
\]
Indeed, \(\chi(r-x)=-\chi(x-r)\), and (6), with shifts \(r\) and \(-t\), gives the value \(-(-1)=1\). Also
\[
f(0)=\chi(r)\chi(t)=1. \tag{8}
\]
Since \(\chi(x)^2\) is \(0\) at \(x=0\) and \(1\) elsewhere, (7) and (8) imply
\[
\sum_{x\in F}\chi(x)^2f(x)=0. \tag{9}
\]

The indicator of \(Q\) is
\[
1_Q(x)=\frac{\chi(x)+\chi(x)^2}{2}. \tag{10}
\]
Likewise, because negation maps \(Q\) bijectively onto the nonsquares,
\[
\sum_{s\in Q}g(-s)
 =\frac12\sum_{x\in F}\bigl(-\chi(x)+\chi(x)^2\bigr)g(x) \tag{11}
\]
for every rational-valued function \(g\).

Using (10),
\[
(AB)_{rt}=\sum_{s\in Q}\chi(r-s)\chi(s+t)
=\frac12\sum_{x\in F}\bigl(\chi(x)+\chi(x)^2\bigr)f(x). \tag{12}
\]
On the other hand, after substituting \(x=-s\) and using \(\chi(-1)=-1\), one obtains
\[
(BA)_{rt}
=\frac12\sum_{x\in F}\bigl(\chi(x)-\chi(x)^2\bigr)f(x). \tag{13}
\]
The difference between (12) and (13) is exactly the sum in (9). Thus \(AB=BA\), proving (5).

Combining (5) with the mixed-column lemma gives the following conclusion:

> If \(S\subseteq Q\) has odd cardinality, the matrix whose \(s\)-th column is \((\chi(r-s))_{r\in Q}\) for \(s\in S\), and \((\chi(r+s))_{r\in Q}\) for \(s\notin S\), has determinant zero. \(\tag{14}\)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3. The case \(p\equiv3\pmod4\)

Now suppose \(p=2m+1\equiv3\pmod4\). Then \(m\) is odd and \(\chi(-1)=-1\). There are exactly \(m\) nonzero squares in \(\mathbf F_p\).

The elements
\[
1^2,2^2,\ldots,m^2
\]
are distinct modulo \(p\): if \(i^2=j^2\), then \(i\equiv j\) or \(i\equiv-j\pmod p\); the latter is impossible for \(1\le i,j\le m\), since \(0<i+j<p\). Thus these elements enumerate the set \(Q\).

The factorial \(C=m!\) is nonzero modulo \(p\). For every \(j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\), exactly one of \(Cj\) and \(-Cj\) is a square, because \(Cj\ne0\) and \(-1\) is a nonsquare. Define
\[
s_j=\begin{cases}
Cj,&\chi(Cj)=1,\\
-Cj,&\chi(Cj)=-1.
\end{cases} \tag{15}
\]
Then \(s_j\in Q\). These \(s_j\)'s are distinct. Indeed, equality of two values in (15), after cancelling \(C\), gives either \(j=k\), \(-j=-k\), or \(j=-k\pmod p\). The first two give \(j=k\), while the last is impossible because \(0<j+k<p\). Therefore (15) also enumerates \(Q\).

Let
\[
S=\{s_j:\chi(Cj)=1\}\subseteq Q.
\]
We next show that \(|S|\) is odd. Put \(g_j=\chi(j)\in\{\pm1\}\) and \(P=\prod_{j=1}^m g_j\). Since \(C=\prod_{j=1}^m j\), multiplicativity gives \(P=\chi(C)\), and hence
\[
\chi(Cj)=P g_j. \tag{16}
\]
For any odd number \(m\) of signs \(g_j\), the number of indices satisfying \(Pg_j=1\) is odd. To see this directly, if \(P=1\), the number of negative signs is even, so the number of positive signs is odd; if \(P=-1\), the number of negative signs is odd, and those are exactly the indices with \(Pg_j=1\). By (16), \(|S|\) is odd.

Reindex the rows of \(L\) by \(r=i^2\in Q\), and its columns by \(s=s_j\in Q\). If \(\chi(Cj)=1\), then \(s=Cj\) and the corresponding entry is
\[
\chi(i^2-Cj)=\chi(r-s)=A_{rs}.
\]
If \(\chi(Cj)=-1\), then \(s=-Cj\) and the entry is
\[
\chi(i^2-Cj)=\chi(r+s)=B_{rs}.
\]
Thus, up to row and column permutations, \(L\) is exactly the mixed Paley matrix in (14), with the odd set of \(A\)-columns \(S\). Therefore
\[
\det L=0 \qquad (p\equiv3\pmod4). \tag{17}
\]
This argument includes \(p=3\): then \(m=C=1\), and the sole entry is \(\chi(1-1)=0\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4. A nonsingularity criterion for power matrices

For the opposite congruence class we need another linear-algebra lemma. Let \(K\) be a field, let \(m>0\), and let
\[
x_1,\ldots,x_m,
\qquad y_1,\ldots,y_m
\]
be two lists of pairwise distinct elements of \(K\). Let \(c\ne0\), suppose
\[
x_i^m=1\quad(1\le i\le m), \tag{18}
\]
and suppose each binomial coefficient \(\binom mr\), \(1\le r<m\), is nonzero in \(K\). If
\[
1-(-c)^m\prod_{j=1}^m(-y_j)\ne0, \tag{19}
\]
then
\[
\det\bigl((x_i-cy_j)^m\bigr)_{1\le i,j\le m}\ne0. \tag{20}
\]

Here is a proof. Define a Vandermonde matrix
\[
V_{ir}=x_i^r\qquad(0\le r<m)
\]
and a second matrix \(H\), with rows indexed by \(0\le r<m\), by
\[
H_{0j}=(-c)^m y_j^m+1,
\]
\[
H_{rj}=\binom mr(-c)^{m-r}y_j^{m-r}\qquad(1\le r<m). \tag{21}
\]
The binomial theorem, with the \(r=m\) term replaced by \(x_i^m=1\) and combined with the \(r=0\) row, gives
\[
(x_i-cy_j)^m=\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}V_{ir}H_{rj}.
\]
Thus the matrix in (20) is \(VH\). The distinctness of the \(x_i\)'s makes the Vandermonde determinant nonzero. It remains to prove that \(H\) is nonsingular.

Suppose a linear combination of its columns, with coefficients \(v_j\), is zero, and put
\[
S_r=\sum_{j=1}^m v_jy_j^r.
\]
Since all factors \(\binom mr(-c)^{m-r}\) in the nonzero rows of (21) are nonzero, the rows \(r=m-s\), for \(1\le s<m\), give
\[
S_s=0\qquad(1\le s<m). \tag{22}
\]
The zeroth row gives
\[
(-c)^mS_m+S_0=0. \tag{23}
\]

Consider the monic polynomial
\[
P(T)=\prod_{j=1}^m(T-y_j)
=T^m+\cdots+\prod_{j=1}^m(-y_j).
\]
For every \(j\), \(P(y_j)=0\). Multiply this equality by \(v_j\), sum over \(j\), and use (22). All intermediate coefficients disappear, leaving
\[
S_m+\left(\prod_{j=1}^m(-y_j)\right)S_0=0. \tag{24}
\]
Substitution of (24) into (23) gives
\[
\left(1-(-c)^m\prod_{j=1}^m(-y_j)\right)S_0=0.
\]
By (19), \(S_0=0\), and then (22) says \(S_r=0\) for every \(0\le r<m\). The Vandermonde matrix built from the distinct \(y_j\)'s is nonsingular, so the only solution of these moment equations is \(v_j=0\) for every \(j\). Hence the columns of \(H\) are linearly independent, \(H\) is nonsingular, and (20) follows.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5. The case \(p\equiv1\pmod4\)

Suppose now that \(p=2m+1\equiv1\pmod4\). Then \(m\) is even. Work in \(K=\mathbf F_p\), and set
\[
x_i=i^2,\qquad y_j=j,
\qquad c=C=m! \pmod p,
\qquad 1\le i,j\le m. \tag{25}
\]
We verify every hypothesis of the power-matrix criterion.

The \(x_i\)'s are pairwise distinct by the same \(i^2=j^2\) argument used above, and the \(y_j\)'s are plainly pairwise distinct modulo \(p\). None of \(1,\ldots,m\) is zero modulo \(p\), and Fermat's theorem gives
\[
x_i^m=(i^2)^m=i^{2m}=i^{p-1}=1. \tag{26}
\]
Also \(C\ne0\pmod p\). For \(1\le r<m\), the binomial coefficient \(\binom mr\) is not divisible by \(p\): indeed, if it were, then from
\[
r!(m-r)!\binom mr=m!
\]
we would obtain \(p\mid m!\), impossible because \(m<p\). Thus all required binomial coefficients are nonzero in \(\mathbf F_p\).

It remains to verify (19). Wilson's theorem yields a useful half-factorial identity. Pair the factors in \((p-1)!\) as \(k\) and \(p-k\), for \(1\le k\le m\). Then
\[
(p-1)!\equiv \prod_{k=1}^m k(-k)=(-1)^m(m!)^2=C^2\pmod p,
\]
because \(m\) is even. Wilson's theorem says \((p-1)!\equiv-1\pmod p\), so
\[
C^2=-1 \quad\text{in }\mathbf F_p. \tag{27}
\]
Moreover,
\[
\prod_{j=1}^m(-y_j)=(-1)^m m!=C. \tag{28}
\]
Suppose, contrary to (19), that
\[
(-C)^m\prod_{j=1}^m(-y_j)=1.
\]
By (28), this is \((-C)^mC=1\). Squaring and using that \(m\) is even and (27), we get
\[
1=\bigl((-C)^mC\bigr)^2=C^{2m+2}=(C^2)^{m+1}=(-1)^{m+1}=-1,
\]
impossible in the odd-characteristic field \(\mathbf F_p\). Thus (19) holds.

The criterion therefore gives
\[
\det\bigl((i^2-Cj)^m\bigr)_{1\le i,j\le m}\ne0
\quad\text{in }\mathbf F_p. \tag{29}
\]
Euler's criterion, including the zero case, says for every \(z\in\mathbf F_p\) that
\[
z^{(p-1)/2}=\chi(z).
\]
Since \(m=(p-1)/2\), the matrix in (29) is precisely the reduction modulo \(p\) of the integer Legendre-symbol matrix \(L\). Hence its determinant is the reduction modulo \(p\) of \(\det L\). If the integer \(\det L\) were zero, its reduction would be zero, contradicting (29). Therefore
\[
\det L\ne0 \qquad (p\equiv1\pmod4). \tag{30}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 6. Completion and the sequence indexing

For \(n\ge2\), let \(p\) be the \(n\)-th prime, equivalently the prime with zero-based index \(n-1\). Since \(n-1\ge1\), we have \(p\ge3\), so \(p\ne2\). Every odd prime is congruent to either \(1\) or \(3\pmod4\). If \(p\equiv3\pmod4\), (17) gives \(a(n)=\det L=0\). Conversely, if \(a(n)=0\), the alternative \(p\equiv1\pmod4\) is excluded by (30), so necessarily \(p\equiv3\pmod4\). Thus, for every \(n\ge2\),
\[
\boxed{\ a(n)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p_n\equiv3\pmod4\ }.
\]
